projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Conny L. Fleissner was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Today is January 23rd, 2009. We are at the Institute of Historical Survey in Las Cruces, New Mexico where veteran Con L. Fleissner will share his military experiences with us. Con Fleissner was born in Waco, Texas on October 31, 1918. He is now ninety years old. He currently lives at 1625 Spruce in Las Cruces, New Mexico. 1625 Spruce, number 31. He was commisioned in the United States Navy as a Reserve and became a Lieutenant JG.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: I was commisioned

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Oh, you were sworn in as an officer. He served during World War II. He was at the Naval Air Station at Kaneohe, Hawaii and Staff COM Air Pacific. Most of his service was done in Hawaii. Alright Con, let's start at the beginning. Would you tell us where you were when you went into the service?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yeah it all got started when I was a ham in 1933. Ham radio operator in high school and then I went to A and M, New Mexico A and M, from 1936 to 1941. I graduated as an electrical engineer. I got a B.S. in electrical engineering. I had arranged a job, my aunt lived in Hollywood and I visited, I arranged a job when I got out of school with Stoddard Aircraft Radio 6630 Santa Monica Boulevard, Hollywood [Laughter]. We were building aircraft radio for ferrying aircrafts to Britain before we entered the war. I worked for them for roughly three years on various projects that were military oriented. When Cassino didn't fall -

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: That was Cassino, Italy?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: That was in 1943, early '43 or late '43. The higher ups in the military decided they wanted more infantrymen. They said everybody twenty-five and under can get in now. My priority wasn't real high. If I had been in radar, I think it would have been continued deferment. I was deferred by the Dona Ana Board #2; it was a draft board in Old Mesilla. I went to the recruiting - I had had ROTC for two years and enjoyed it, so I went to the Army recruiting center in Los Angeles in downtown Los Angeles; what's that called, the square. They said, "Unless you're a preacher or a surgeon, we're not taking you today. Go home and we'll draft you." So I went out and across the way was the Navy recruiting. I thought, well I'll go over and see what they have. I went over there and they said, "What do you do?" I said, "I'm a radio engineer." "Oh! Come in!" [Laughter] And in about forty five minutes I had a written exam, an oral exam, and kind of a physical exam for commission. They said, "We're putting you in the radar training program." It was necessary to run clearance in those days so they told me to go home and they would advise me when the clearance came through, which it did in about three or four weeks. In the meantime, they said, "If they draft you, ask for the Navy group." I was really kind of interested in the Army, and I hesitated. They said, "Well, if you get into the Army and the commission comes through it's at the discretion of the Army commander as to whether he would release you. However, if you're in the Navy as an enlisted, it's an order from the Secretary of the Navy and then you'd be commissioned." So anyway, I took the draft physical which is one of the best I ever had and at the end of the deal the Navy said, "Well, our quota is filled." It was late in the afternoon. I told them the story and they said, "Okay well that's different; we'll put you down for the Navy contingent." However, the commission came through before they called me. Then I went to Fort Schuyler for training for two months indoctrination.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And Fort Schuyler is in New York City, right?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: In the Bronx, New York, right at the junction of the East River and the Long Island Sound. From there, after that we went to Harvard University there in Cambridge. We were there October, November, December, January; I guess four months there.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Was there very good training?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yeah, in basic electronics with emphasis on sonar graphs and cathode ray type. They put us up in Gore Hall. Do you know where that is on Harvard?

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: It's right on the river there. They provided room and board there at Gore Hall, it was very nice student quarters. After that period we were assigned to the M.I.T. Radar Program, which was conducted in the Harbor Building near South Station in Boston. Do you know Boston?

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: No, not very well.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Okay, well it's by South Station in Boston and we had four more months there; very good airborne, my group was airborne radar - very excellent professors, some military and some civilian, but it was a very good program. A little sideline, there was also an Army program going on. Professor Harold Brown from New Mexico A and M was teaching in that group. He and I - he had been a professor of mine and we were very good friends. He visited when I lived in California and so on.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: It really is a small world.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: They had a small coffee shop, but the students weren't supposed to go there. But I would go as his guest. The director of our group had a very good looking secretary, and I thought, "I ought to ask her for a date." Well before I got around to it, she asked me, which was very flattering. I asked her, "Well, how did you choose me?" She said, "I went through the files and you were one of the few single men." [Laughter] That deflated me. So anyway, we finished our training there, and we were assigned to Pearl Harbor. We flew from San Francisco to Pearl.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And you flew?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Another sideline, we were quartered in a hotel in San Francisco for about a week, and there was a launch over at Alameda where we left for Hawaii, and I think it was just another ensign and I were the only two on that launch. I said, "Well, a week is enough in San Francisco. How long have you been here?" And he said, "You know those civilian girls who were checking us in?" I said, "Yes, I remember them." He said, "Well, I started dating one of them, and she couldn't find space available for me. So I have been here for thirty days." [Laughter] That's a good one. The orders read, "Space Available." Later we were quartered at Ford Island, right next to where the Arizona went down. Our assignment was to check in once a day for orders. After I had been there a day or two, maybe three or four, one of my classmates said he was going over to Kaneohe for an interview - major radar overhaul. He said, "Do you want to come along?" I said, "Might as well, I don't have anything to do except check in once a day." So, I went over with him. I think we took a commercial bus, we had to go over the pass in those days. Now they have a tunnel. We went over there and he went in for an interview. He was gone for twenty-five minutes or so with the officer in charge. I sat outside and read a magazine. The kid came out with the officer in charge and saw me sitting there. He said, "What have you been doing?" I said, "Well I worked for Stoddard Aircraft, a small outfit, fifty or sixty people." Two or three days later I get called to take the job there at the radar overhaul and this classmate of mine got shipped out to the Philippines - where it was dangerous, there was war going on and Kamikazes were coming in. [Laughter] It was just fate. So that's how I fluked into that job there.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Now this was not at Pearl Harbor, this was at Kaneohe?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: On the other side of the island, the other side of Oahu.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What were your duties?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Well, we were supervising the overhaul testing of radio and radar equipment. I had a group of roughly one hundred people, most of them military but there were a few civilians also in the group, there. That went on for a couple of months, and then the war ended and we continued to do that work.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Who was using this radar equipment?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Navy aircraft.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: So this was Naval aircraft?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yes. We were airborne types.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Where did you live when you were working on radar?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Well, we first lived in "termite village", [Laughter] that's what we called it. There were three of us quartered in a small apartment, a two-bedroom apartment. After the war was over, pretty shortly they started bringing families in. We had to - we were evicted from termite village. Then we had to live in the B.O.Q.; the mess was there, of course.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: So you were fed and housed?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yes, and then probably about April of '45 - no, April of '46. The war ended in '45. March or April they closed down the facility, overhaul. I was out of a job so I understood they were going to put me in as the manager of the B.O.Q.; they had a Reserve Full Commander in charge of a B.O.Q. of maybe three hundred rooms, like a hotel. A lot of [inaudible] going through there. I really didn't know anything about the hotel business. One of my secretaries' husband was on the staff, so I called her and said, "See what you can do for me." [Laughter] So they put me on the Comair Pac as a, I think they called me an Assistant Com Officer, Communications Officer, but I was really a consultant. They wanted to know who had cognizance of the various electronic equipment in the Comair Pac deal which included Johnson Island, and Midway Island and all of the Hawaiian group. I think Palmyra Island, too, though I didn't get to Palmyra.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What exactly was Comair Pac?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: That was the Commander of Air Pacific. Yes.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And your job then, was to work on the communications?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: It was really a consultant - see what's going on. Who had cognizance of what equipment on the various islands. During the war, things got a little jumbled up there. There was Army, and Navy, and Coast Guard involved in the various communication facilities and aids, beacons and so forth. They didn't know who owned what, or who was really in charge. So they sent me around to check on various things and then report what was going on.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Did you have any interesting experiences going from island to island?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yeah, on Midway we were talking with the Chief about one of the transmitter facilities there and we were looking at the various transmitters and so on. He pushed a button and a light came on that said, "Tilt" and he just said, "Those damn kids there." [Laughter] I thought that was kind of funny and incongruous, out there with the goony birds and so forth. And with equipment that, when you press a button, it says, "Tilt," somebody had a sense of humor. Then they had a naval air transport that served there, I think twice a week. I got through there after maybe a week. I was waiting to get back, and the Marines came by in an R-D and I said, "Can I hitch a ride?" They said, "Yeah, we're having a little engine trouble but we think we'll make it." I said, "You'll make it without me, I'm not going!" [Laughter] I wasn't too -

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: You weren't that eager to get back?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: There's a lot of water between Midway and Hawaii. I finally did get a ride from a Marine four-engine plane, about a day later. [End Of Side One]

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Alright, so you finally got back from Midway to Oahu.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Let's see - Comair Pac was at Pearl Harbor. I ran across a fraternity brother who had gone to Anapolis, and he was the engineering officer on the submarine Sea Fox. This was after the war, they had just come back from major overhaul at Hunter's Point. He said, "How about coming for a ride for a day or two? We're going out on practice." I said, "Great, I'd like to go." Well, unfortunately they sent me out to Midway and I never did get to see them; when I got back, they were long gone.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Oh, so you missed out? Conny Feissner: Recently, on ham radio they have a submariner's net and I was listening to that. I broke in and said I was wondering if anybody knew about the Sea Fox or Willet White. I did find a fellow who had served with him; a quartermaster. He had been on watch with White and he said he had died about fifteen years ago. That was kind of interesting. I went to Johnson Island too, do you know where that is? It's out about eight hundred miles west of Hawaii, we had to survey that area. The captain in charge there was a Reserve. I was there four or five days and we had to get together for coffee like this. We had toast and butter and fresh coffee every morning. I got to know the staff there, the executive officer, and we were having trouble getting a replacement for this captain, "See if you can talk him into staying longer on Johnson Island." So after a few days of getting to know him, I said, "Captain, would you consider staying a while here?" He said, "You go back and tell those son of a bitches to get me off this rock." [Laughter] All I could say was, "Yes, sir." About two or three weeks later I happened to be in the office and he came in, "See I told you I'd get out of that damn place." Johnson Island was a very small island with a runway on one side and then kind of a triangular arrangement for taxi ways.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What would the men do on Johnson Island? Other than work, were there any recreational activities?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yeah, movies at night. [Laughter] They had a bunch of contract laborers from the island of Funi - Funi [?] wherever that is, in the Marianas somewhere. They did laboring work there, and they gave them room and board and a salary, and shoes, because the coral was very hard on shoes. They had one common mess; everybody ate at the same mess. There wasn't any officer's mess. Including the contract laborers. After that, they sat around and tossed a ball around in a circle, and then the movies started. That was the only recreation. I guess fishing, maybe too. I guess that has been expanded now when they carried out tests in the atomic days nearby there. It was practically nothing out there, only a couple of feet above sea level. That was kind of interesting.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: How about your time when you were at Pearl? How did you spend your free time?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: I didn't have much. I served for more than a year with no leave. I wanted to go on leave a couple of times, and then something came up and they couldn't do it. Occasionally I might get a Sunday off. Also, they said, "Well, you're single so you can have the duty, weekends and holidays." [Laughter] So, but I did have a couple of Sundays I think where I went to the beach; there was a commissioned officer's club we used to go there. April 1st, the tsunami hit. That's when they invented it. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: That was about '45?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: '46, yeah. Probably about eight o'clock in the morning I looked out at our overhaul facility, and I turn back and the place was filled with water. "What's going on?" But I found out that the tsunami had hit. It did damage depending on where the reefs were and so on. A lot of people in Hilo were killed and floated out. The air sea rescue people found some people floating on debris out there a day or two later. There was an NRL, Naval Research Lab who was running a project on ducting, radar ducting [?], you'll get false echoes between Oahu and the island of Hawaii. All their equipment was inundated I think.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: There was a lot of flooding on the outer islands, wasn't there?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: It depended on where the reefs were, apparently. But anyway, I heard of their plight and I said, "Well, I've got some ovens here. We'll wash down the equipment and then we'll bake them." So we sent a couple of trucks down; we got their equipment and washed them down with clean water and baked them at a low temperature for about a day or two and about ninety percent of the stuff worked just fine. They were able to continue those tests, that was kind of neat to see.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Was there any damage to your particular facility?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: No, except for the flooding on the tarmac. There were a couple of doctors there that I became good friends with. They brought their wives there, and they rented a cottage in Kailua and the water came up to their doorstep but never came in. They were really lucky on that. People were saved depending on the configurations of the reef and so on.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Terrific. Very good. The Navy food is very, very good. I gained about twenty pounds, I think. I ran across that just recently. I weighed one hundred and fifty five pounds when I went in, I saw the medical record. When I came out I weighed about one hundred and seventy or something like that. I'm down to a hundred and sixty five right now.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: How long were you at that station?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: About fourteen to fifteen months.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Then I was relieved, separated. I wasn't discharged, I was in the Naval Reserve for ten years until 1954 but I was inactive. I probably would have been called back during the Korean War, but a little later they had me listed as ground support aviation instead of electronics. Had I been listed as electronics, they probably would have called me back because I had friends who were called back who were in late in the war like I was. One fellow, who was the ship type, Manual DeLarno from New Orleans, he was called back and joined the ship in Korea. They were only there for a day or two and they went back to Norfolk for overhaul. [Laughter] And, then the C.O. there - in the Navy the C.O. is like God - he said, "You're the engineering officer?" He said, "Hey, I'm in radar I don't know anything about ships!" "Well, you're going to learn!" During engineering it was the skipper, the exec, then the engineering officer. That's the sequence in the Navy. He said, "It wouldn't have been so bad if you had experienced chiefs," But they had manuals. This guy was pretty sharp, so he learned. They sent him to the Mediterranean. He had his wife come over, and he spent the Korean War in the Mediterranean which would be pretty nice.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: When you were separated from the service, where were you separated from?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Los Angeles.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And then what did you do next?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Then I went to Las Cruces and we got together with Dr. Gardner and Professor Brown.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What prompted you to come to Las Cruces?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: I got a wire from Professor Brown, "Don't take any offer until you hear ours."

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: You came to Las Cruces, New Mexico, and why did they want to see you?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: They wanted to start this R and D lab. Dr. Gardner did.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What was Dr. Gardner's first name, Robert?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: George Gardner. I think he was a Nova Scotian, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And this would be an R and D Lab?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yes, he was head of the physics department.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What did they have you do?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: They had me organize, eventually, the lab. I said, "That's a good idea but what do I do for people?" And they said, "You have friends, haven't you?" And what can you say. [Laughter] Well I went back east then; they knew I was going to New York to visit this girl I had been courting there at Wellesley. He said, "Stop in Silver Spring and see Dr. Goss," who had been at the college here. He was working for APL, the Applied Physics Lab, "and see if we can work something with a contract for them." I agreed to do that. I got back to New York after visiting in Silver Spring and a side trip to see a rocket shoot. The girl said, "So sorry, I met this other fellow." [Laughter] Then I went back to Park Ridge, where my folks were.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Is that in Illinois?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Park Ridge, Illinois, yeah. Right near where O'Hare is. I took some flying lessons then. This was September. I had about eight hours in, I was ready to solo and then I got word from Gardner that I had to go to work October 1st. We had negotiated for salary and so forth. I had to go to work. So my orders were to go to Silver Springs and see what I could learn. [Laughter] That was it. No money, no nothing just go. I went to Silver Springs, I was there about five weeks trying to get a feel for what's going on in telemetry.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: That's what they were working on?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: That was some of it, yeah. Then they also had some equipment in Chicago. They had been involved in the proximity fuse, you know what that is?

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Well, it's fusing for shells that would explode when it got near some metal or something. They had developed that. They had a firm in Chicago that had mechanical equipment shop, and plus electronic testing equipment. They said we could have that too if we could have it arranged to get that shipped. I started after I came back from Silver Springs, I came through Chicago and made arrangements to get this equipment to ship it to the college. I bought a car then, too. I asked my mother, "Do you want to drive down with me?" And she said, "Well, if my girlfriend next door will go, I will go." So she agreed. They were ready to go, and the two women, "When are we going to go?" "Pretty soon!" This went on for about ten days. "Maybe tomorrow." [Laughter] Eventually we got going and the first fellow I hired was Calvin Rickets, who eventually became the director of -

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And what did you call this lab?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: PSL, Physical Science Laboratory. This was a fellow officer I had met in Hawaii. Then the first technician I hired was Al Antonis, who was Katy Griggs' second husband. Did you know Katy?

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Yes, I knew her.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: That was her second husband.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: How many people did you hire to start the lab, all total?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Well, first there was myself and Rickets, Antonis, a machine shop man, McFarland, and then Gardner hired Kinetta who was kind of the officer manager. Then we hired another engineer, Richard Olemacher. He was the antenna man. There were half a dozen or eight.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: So fewer than a dozen people?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Sure. It was interesting; this woman friend of my mother's, the next door neighbor, came down, or drove down, and Brown lived on University at that time with his folks. They had a house there, and they weren't there. He said, "Well, why don't you stay here for the night?" With my mother and her girlfriend. Then I guess they took a train or a bus back to Albuquerque and so on. So a year or two later - this woman was from Winnetka, Illinois although she was living in Park Ridge right next to my folks. She was at some affair there in Winnetka with this woman, and she said, "How's your son?" She said, "He's down in school; you wouldn't know it - it's down in New Mexico, Las Cruces." She said, "We were down there just recently and met the nicest professor there, Professor Brown he showed us around." And Kay said, "Oh, we stayed at his house!" [Laughter] Strange coincidence.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: How long did you stay at PSL?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Two years. Exactly two years. October of '48.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: I went to Albuquerque. I got married, and started a business all at one time. When you're young, you can do things like that.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Did you stay in Albuquerque?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yes, about twenty-five years. I started the first electronics firm. Engineering and manufacturing in Albuquerque.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: So that was your business, electronics?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yeah. Crown Engineering, it was called.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Did you have any contact with military people at that time?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yes, we did work for White Sands, Holloman, Sandia, Los Alamos, Hughes Aircraft, National Bureau of Standards, Boeing. I sold off too much stock, and they ousted me, which was bad because I was still the largest stockholder, but the company went belly up after a couple of years; it was bad news. I had a cottage at Elephant Butte. I was doing some rep work. My wife had divorced me, so I started selling real estate there, building house and doing a little electrical work. Then this young couple I met in 1980 that were on a mining venture. We became quite good friends, and I visited them back in the Boston area. In 1990 I visited there. I went down to the Harbor building where we had gone to MIT School. The South Station which is there, that area had been re worked. It was a crummy area in the war days. I said, "I wonder how this gal got along..." I called the alumni office at Wellesley and they said, "Why do you want to know?" I said, "I'm just curious... How she got along..." They said, "Well, the privacy act. However, if you'll send a letter, we'll forward it," which I eventually did. I got a letter back from her that said she had been widowed about ten years before, she was coming to Santa Fe to take some painting lessons and meet her sister from Iowa. So we got together in Albuquerque and about a year later we were married. She was living in Santa Barbara.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Did you stay in Elephant Butte after your marriage?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: No, we moved to her house in Santa Barbara. I was there for ten years. She died about a year before. She died from too much smoking, unfortunately. She was a "travel junky."

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: I was going to say, you did a lot of traveling, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: We went to Europe nine times in nine years, and that doesn't include South Africa, China, Jamaica, Mexico four times, and the U.S. literally from Seattle to Maine. Not figuratively, literally. [Laughter]

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Were you still working with radio during your travelling days?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: No, well, I set up a ham station in Santa Barbara. Yes.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Con, did you keep in touch with any of the men you had known in the service?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: I saw the Executive Officer that I served under back in Washington, a Captain Huff. I can't remember exactly what year that was, like 1950 or something of that sort, maybe a little later. I had lunch with him, and he acted like he had arthritis. I said, "Captain..." he had been my chief at Brussels and he was a very good man. I said, "Do you have arthritis?" He said, "No, my son had a paper route, and he's been ill so I had to take his paper route for a couple of weeks." [Laughter] My old captain.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Did you join any military organizations?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yes. When I was at Elephant Butte there, I sold a piece of property to the command of one of the VFW's. Part of the deal was that I join the VFW. At that time, Hawaii was considered overseas duty; it was a territory it wasn't a state, so. I was eligible on that basis. I was getting pretty old, and they had the lifetime deal there for I can't remember, a hundred and fifty dollars or so, and I said, "Sign me up for a lifetime." So I joined that, a lifetime member.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: When did you move to Las Cruces this time?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: In 2002, I became homeless. We had a prenuptial agreement, but they wanted me out early, the children - because of the income from the property, which only brought 1.4 million, and the children are allergic to work. She had three children and none of them work. [Laughter] So I became homeless then, and I spent my first couple of nights in Las Vegas. All I had was a car, a radio, a computer, some clothes and a towel, I think. It was quite a shock, you know. First it was a couple of nights in Las Vegas, and then a couple of nights at Laughlin. Where else can you get a fifteen dollar room, you know? I came back to Cruces by way of Silver City; I have a daughter in Silver. I decided to reside here because of my age and the transportation and all of that.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Not a bad climate either.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Well, you've had quite an interesting life both in and out of the service. But as you look back on the young Con Fleissner who went into the service, how would you say that time in the service influenced you either as a person or with what you did with your life?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Well, the training was excellent. The radar, I was familiar with radar then and in my operation there in Crown Engineering we kind of fluked into a job of a Titan 1 missile, in Denver. I took over from a contractor who didn't understand radar and how to handle the stuff. Really, we were going on vacation with the family and one of my engineers had a friend working at Martin, and he said, "Drop by and see him." I said, "Well, we're going on vacation but we will go and see him anyway." So we went by Denver, and they were having a problem with this contractor. They said, "Do you have any security clearance?" And I was really anxious to get going. I said, "Well, I had some in Dallas." The security man from Dallas, I guess his wife was a good Baptist, and we became friends when he dropped into see me. If he had business or if he didn't have business about four thirty he would call and say, "Hey can you have a couple of beers with me?" So anyway, one day they apparently called Dallas, and they came back in about ten minutes and looked at me like I must be next to God or something. Apparently this fellow gave me a clean bill of health. We got this job; we took this job on a time and material basis to continue the assembly of this test stand. We had four test stands, it was an instrument then with our wave guide. Then we finished the job, I think, it was seventy-two thousand, and they wrote the contract for seventy-five thousand. They said, "When you get near the end, let us know and we'll fund it for more." Well, I finished at less than that, and they didn't like it. It made them look bad. So anyway, they had more work then. There were three of us with a couple of big outfits and myself bidding on the bigger job, which ran about a quarter of a million. It was on a different basis, on a cost plus. So I came in just slightly lower on the bidding, I learned this later on and so they said, "We don't want him in there. We'll rebid for an accelerated delivery." Well, Martin was going to supply about half the parts and I had to supply the other half. I knew Martin couldn't do it; they didn't do it the first time, there's no reason they'd do it the second time. So I cut my price slightly, for car rentals and per diem and so on. The other two contractors went up in price, for overtime. They had to award the contract to me. I learned this later on through the purchasing branch[?] so we had that. They said, "We've got this test down in Florida that needs to be instrumented." In Cape Canaveral. That was before Kennedy. And why don't you go down and look at that job? It was a long ways away. They said, "Well, we've got a plane leaving Tuesday afternoon, go down to the airport and get on there." So I did that. There were about twenty-five of us on the plane. We came around with the manifest and they said, "What's your name?" I said, "Fleissner." "Well, you're not on here." I said, "I guess they forgot it." And they put me down, so I went to Florida in the Martin plane and we got the job of instrumenting the test stand for Martin down there. Then there was a blow-up, so we had another one to do there. That was - I sent a crew down there.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: What did you when you instrumented a test stand?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Well we were providing microwave lines. They were circular and rectangular wave guides.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: And this was for rockets?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: For the launching, yes. Titan 1 continental missile.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Well, as you know, your story is going to be a part of American history.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: [Laughter] For what it's worth.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: But people who were not alive during these years, and some who are not alive today, will be reading your information or listening to it. You have any thing you'd like to say to future generations?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to say to future generations?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Well, yeah. Education pays off really well, and the part of the education of ham radio provides a good starting place for young people. Certainly education is worthwhile, and I owe a lot to the university here, the education was excellent. In those days, we were really embarrassed into learning. The classes were so small that they knew you by your first name. They called on you for recitation about every day, so you had to be prepared.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Now, you attended New Mexico A and M which is now New Mexico State University. Here in Las Cruces, New Mexico.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Is there anything else you'd like to say?

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: I can't think of anything else.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Alright.

sp.speaker: Conny L. Fleissner
sp.p: It was a very enjoyable life; there's been a lot of variety, and it's been very enjoyable.

sp.speaker: Louise S. Forshaw
sp.p: Fascinating variety, I'd say. Well, we thank you, Con Fleissner for your interview. This completes our interview with Con J. Fleissner.
